title: Criminal vs civil law
examples: What is the difference between a civil case and a criminal case?
Who has to prove something in a court?
What happens if someone is found not guilty?

explain.say: Today we will look at two types of law. These are criminal law and civil law.
The burden of proof is who must prove the case. In criminal law, the state must prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

draw.text: Burden of Proof: Beyond a reasonable doubt

explain.say: In civil law, the burden of proof is usually on the person who is suing. They must prove their claim on the balance of probabilities.
The outcomes are very different too. Criminal cases can result in jail time. Civil cases usually result in money payments.
Consider a shoplifting case. If the state brings charges, it is criminal law. If you sue for lost goods, it is civil law.

items: Suing for goods | Lost goods | Civil

explain.say: A common mistake is assuming all disputes are criminal. Remember the difference in who is suing and what they want.

draw.text: Mistake: Assuming all cases are criminal

faq.q: If someone breaks a law, is it always a criminal case?
faq.a: Not always. Sometimes the damage caused is just between two people. The state might not get involved at all.
asks: Must breaking a law mean a criminal case?

faq.q: What does 'beyond a reasonable doubt' actually mean in court?
faq.a: It means the jury must be very sure of the defendant's guilt. They cannot guess; they need strong proof.
asks: How sure does the state have to be?
What is the standard for criminal proof?

faq.q: If I win a civil case, do I get to jail time?
faq.a: No. Civil cases are about compensation, usually money. Jail time is reserved for criminal offenses.
asks: Can civil law result in imprisonment?
What is the punishment in civil court?

faq.q: Who decides if a case is criminal or civil?
faq.a: The parties involved or the police usually decide this at the start. The nature of the dispute guides the type of law.
asks: Who decides the type of case?
Can a case switch from civil to criminal?

faq.q: What is the difference between 'guilt' and 'liability'?
faq.a: Guilt relates to breaking the law against society. Liability relates to being legally responsible for damages to another person.
asks: What is the difference between criminal and civil fault?
Does liability mean you broke a law?

facts: Criminal law deals with actions that harm the public or state.
Civil law deals with disputes between private individuals or groups.
Criminal cases require proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
Civil cases require proof on the balance of probabilities.

quiz.say: A neighbour sues you because your fence caused damage to their garden. Is this likely criminal or civil law?
quiz.why: This is a dispute between two neighbours over property damage, not a crime against the state.

wrong.0: This is tempting because breaking property can be illegal, but the action here is a private dispute.
wrong.1: This is wrong because the nature of the dispute clearly points to a private remedy.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the primary focus is on compensation between parties, not state punishment.

quiz.say: If the state prosecutes someone for theft, what standard of proof must they meet?
quiz.why: Because the state is accusing someone of breaking a major law, the proof required is the highest standard.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it suggests a low standard of proof, which is inappropriate for criminal law.
wrong.2: This is wrong because that standard is used for private civil claims, not state accusations.
wrong.3: This is wrong because legal standards are based on evidence, not simple majority opinion.

quiz.say: A person is found liable for negligence in a car accident. What is the most likely outcome?
quiz.why: Negligence is a civil matter where one person compensates another for losses, usually with money.

wrong.0: This is wrong because jail time is reserved for criminal offenses, not just civil negligence.
wrong.1: This is wrong because while warnings happen, the primary legal remedy for damages is financial compensation.
wrong.2: This is wrong because being found liable means the law has determined fault and requires a remedy.
